definition: Movement of a limb away from the body's midline, as when raising an arm out to the side.
The process by which digested nutrients pass from the gut into the blood or lymph for use by cells.
Movement of a limb toward the body's midline, as when lowering a raised arm back to your side.
A type of connective tissue packed with fat-storing cells, cushioning organs, insulating the body, and holding a reserve of energy.
The muscle that produces a particular movement, often called the prime mover, such as the biceps in a curl.
One of millions of tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves the blood.
The standard reference posture: standing upright, face forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward, and feet pointing forward.
A muscle that opposes the action of another muscle, helping control and reverse a movement, as the triceps opposes the biceps.
Toward the front of the body, or nearer the belly side, as the sternum lies anterior to the heart.
A Y-shaped protein made by immune cells that locks onto a specific invader and helps mark it for destruction.
A thick-walled blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart and toward the body's tissues.
Adenosine triphosphate, the small molecule that stores and releases energy for nearly every activity inside a cell.
Listening to sounds inside the body, usually with a stethoscope, to assess the heart, lungs, or intestines.
The part of the nervous system that regulates involuntary body functions such as heart rate, digestion, and sweating without conscious effort.
Relating to both sides of the body, as when a rash appears on both arms in a similar pattern.
Removal of a small sample of tissue so a specialist can examine its cells under a microscope.
The fluid connective tissue that carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, and immune cells through vessels to organs throughout the body.
The force blood exerts against vessel walls, recorded as two numbers that reflect the heart's contracting and relaxing phases.
A hard living tissue reinforced with calcium phosphate minerals that supports the body, protects organs, and houses red marrow that makes blood cells.
The smallest blood vessel, a thin-walled tube where oxygen and nutrients pass into tissues and waste passes from tissues into the blood.
A firm, flexible tissue that pads joints, shapes the nose and ears, and forms a temporary skeleton in early development.
Toward the tail or lower end of the body, a term used mainly in embryology and comparative anatomy.
The selective outer boundary of a cell, a thin film of fat and protein that controls what enters and leaves.
The brain and spinal cord, the control center that processes information and coordinates the rest of the nervous system.
A circular movement in which a limb sweeps through a cone-shaped path, combining flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction.
Body material that supports, binds, or separates other structures, ranging from soft padding to strong tendons and solid bone.
On the opposite side of the body, as when a stroke weakens the arm on the side opposite the damaged half of the brain.
A vertical plane that divides the body into front and back portions, also called the frontal plane.
Toward the head or skull end of the body, as the cranial end of the spinal cord sits nearest the brain.
A slice cut through a structure, usually at right angles to its long axis, revealing its internal arrangement.
Computed tomography, a scan that combines X-ray images from many angles into detailed cross-sectional pictures of the body.
The jelly-like fluid and structures inside a cell, where many chemical reactions and much of the cell's work happen.
Farther beneath the body's surface, as a deep muscle sits under layers of skin and fat.
A downward movement of a body part, such as lowering the shoulders or opening the jaw.
The relaxation phase of the heart cycle, when the chambers fill with blood before the next contraction.
The natural spreading of particles from crowded areas to less crowded ones, such as oxygen moving into a cell.
The breakdown of food into small molecules that can be absorbed, beginning in the mouth and continuing through the gut.
Farther from the point where a limb attaches to the body, as the fingers are distal to the elbow.
The long, twisted-ladder molecule in nearly every cell that stores the instructions for building proteins and running the body.
Toward the back of the body, as the dorsal surface of the hand is the side with the fingernails.
Bending the foot upward toward the shin, as when you stand on your heels or lift your toes.
An upward movement of a body part, such as shrugging the shoulders or closing the jaw.
A procedure in which a tube with a camera and light, often flexible, is passed into the body to view internal organs directly.
A molecule, usually a protein, that speeds up a specific chemical reaction, such as breaking down food or copying DNA, without being used up.
A sheet of cells that covers surfaces, lines cavities, and forms glands, serving as a barrier and handling absorption or secretion.
A red blood cell, a flexible disc packed with hemoglobin that carries oxygen from the lungs to tissues.
Turning the sole of the foot outward, away from the body's midline, as when rolling onto the inner edge of the foot.
The removal of waste products from the body, such as urea filtered by the kidneys or carbon dioxide exhaled by the lungs.
Straightening a joint so the angle between two body parts increases, as when you open a bent elbow.
A sheet or band of tough connective tissue that wraps muscles, organs, and nerves, holding them in place.
The moment a sperm and egg join to form a single cell, the first step in the development of a new organism.
The process of forcing fluid through a barrier that catches larger particles, as the kidneys filter blood.
Bending a joint so the angle between two body parts decreases, as when you bring your hand toward your shoulder.
The period during which an embryo or fetus develops in the uterus, about nine months in humans.
The iron-containing protein inside red blood cells that binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues.
A liver cell, specialized for processing nutrients, detoxifying harmful substances, and making bile and blood proteins.
The body's ability to keep internal conditions such as temperature, pH, and blood sugar within a narrow, stable range.
A chemical messenger released by a gland or cell that travels in the blood and alters the activity of target cells.
A clean cut made through skin or tissue, often by a surgeon, to reach a structure beneath the surface.
Below or lower than another structure in the body, as the stomach is inferior to the heart.
The body's local response to injury or infection, marked by redness, heat, swelling, and pain.
The end of a muscle that attaches to the bone that moves when the muscle contracts.
Turning the sole of the foot inward, toward the body's midline, as when rolling onto the outer edge of the foot.
On the same side of the body, as when a muscle and the nerve controlling it sit on the same side.
The place where two or more bones meet; movable joints are shaped for motion and cushioned by cartilage.
A surgical technique that uses a slender camera and small instruments through tiny incisions in the abdomen.
Away from the body's midline or toward the side, as the ears are lateral to the nose.
A tough band of connective tissue that links bone to bone and holds joints steady.
A clear fluid that drains from tissues, carries immune cells, and returns slowly to the bloodstream.
A small, bean-shaped checkpoint where lymph is filtered and immune cells gather to meet invading microbes.
A network of vessels, nodes, and organs that drains lymph and helps defend the body against infection.
Toward the body's midline, as the big toe is on the medial side of the foot.
The sum of all chemical reactions in the body that build molecules and release energy from food.
A vertical plane that divides the body into equal left and right halves along the body's midline.
A bean-shaped structure inside cells that uses oxygen and food to generate usable energy for the cell.
Magnetic resonance imaging, a scan that uses strong magnets and radio waves to build detailed images of soft tissue.
A moist lining that covers internal surfaces such as the mouth, nose, and gut, and secretes mucus.
A type of body tissue made of cells that contract, often in response to nerve signals, producing movement and maintaining posture.
The microscopic filtering unit of the kidney, which removes waste from blood and balances water and salts.
A nerve cell that receives, processes, and transmits electrical signals to other cells throughout the nervous system.
A chemical released at a synapse that carries a signal from one neuron to another neuron, a muscle cell, or a gland cell.
The control center of a cell, a membrane-bound compartment that holds DNA and directs the cell's activities.
A slanted plane that cuts through the body at an angle, neither purely vertical nor horizontal.
A structure made of several tissues that works together to perform a particular job, such as the heart or liver.
The end of a muscle that stays relatively fixed on bone when the muscle contracts.
The movement of water across a membrane that lets water pass but blocks some dissolved particles, flowing toward a more concentrated solution and balancing fluids inside and outside cells.
Examining the body by feeling its surface with the hands to check size, texture, tenderness, or position.
Wave-like muscle contractions that push food through the digestive tract, from the esophagus to the colon.
Pointing the foot downward, as when standing on tiptoe or pushing off the ground to walk.
The pale yellow liquid part of blood, carrying dissolved nutrients, hormones, and waste while blood cells float in it.
Toward the back of the body, or nearer the back surface, as the spine lies posterior to the stomach.
Rotating the forearm so the palm turns downward or backward, as when placing a hand flat on a table.
Lying face down, with the chest and belly against the surface and the back facing upward.
Moving a body part forward, usually in a flat path, as when pushing the jaw or shoulders ahead.
Closer to the point where a limb attaches to the body, as the shoulder is proximal to the elbow.
The technique of producing images with X-rays, showing dense structures such as bone as bright shapes.
The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the air, blood, and cells, plus the processes that use oxygen.
Moving a body part backward, usually in a flat path, as when pulling the jaw or shoulders back.
Turning a body part around its own long axis, as when shaking your head no from side to side.
A vertical plane that divides the body into left and right portions; the name comes from the Latin word for arrow.
The release of useful substances from a cell, such as hormones into blood or mucus onto a surface.
A thin, smooth sheet that lines body cavities and covers organs, releasing fluid that reduces friction.
Muscle attached to bone by tendons that produces voluntary movement and is marked by light and dark stripes.
Involuntary muscle found in the walls of the gut, blood vessels, and bladder, contracting slowly and steadily.
Closer to the body's surface, as a superficial cut involves skin but not deeper tissue.
Above or higher than another structure in the body, as the heart is superior to the stomach.
Rotating the forearm so the palm turns upward or forward, as when holding out a hand to catch something.
Lying face up, with the back against the surface and the face toward the ceiling.
A stitch that joins the edges of a wound or surgical cut; in the skull, the same word also names the fibrous seams between bones.
The tiny junction where a neuron passes a signal to another cell, usually by releasing a chemical messenger.
The contracting phase of the heart cycle, when chambers pump blood out into the arteries.
A strong cord of connective tissue that attaches a muscle to bone and carries its pull.
A group of similar cells that work together on a shared task, such as lining a surface or transmitting signals.
A horizontal plane that divides the body into upper and lower portions, like a belt line.
An imaging technique that sends high-frequency sound waves into the body and builds pictures from the echoes.
A blood vessel that carries blood back toward the heart, usually containing oxygen-poor blood from the tissues.
Toward the front or belly side of the body, as the abdominal organs sit in the ventral cavity.
One of many tiny finger-like projections in the small intestine that greatly increase the surface for absorbing nutrients.
A form of high-energy radiation that passes easily through soft tissue but is blocked by bone, producing an image of dense internal structures.
The single cell formed when a sperm and egg fuse, which divides repeatedly to begin a new organism.
